faq.answer: Repeatedly choosing to help in comparable situations can support a limited description of your helping tendency. Still ask whether agreement was voluntary and what resources were available. Concern, duty, habit and discomfort with refusal can coexist; frequent agreement alone does not establish effective help or reveal every motive.
faq.question: Does frequently saying yes establish high Altruism?

faq.answer: Not necessarily. You may lack capacity or capability, find the request unsuitable, or know that the person does not want that kind of help. You may also not wish to undertake it. Describe the actual reason rather than drawing a broad character judgment from one refusal.
faq.question: Does refusing a request mean I do not care?

faq.answer: No. Desire and capability need separate evidence. Check what the task requires, what resources you have, whether help is welcome and what the result was. Enthusiasm does not substitute for those conditions.
faq.question: Does a strong willingness to help mean I am good at helping?

faq.answer: The facet does not establish that skill. Making fewer spontaneous offers is different from clearly communicating and enforcing limits. People anywhere along the range can overcommit or leave their scope unclear.
faq.question: Are people with lower Altruism better at boundaries?

faq.answer: They cannot establish trait change on their own. A deliberate attempt can tell you about consent, communication, usefulness and cost. Keep it separate from natural offers, and include opportunities where no offer occurred as well as occasions without a suitable opportunity.
faq.question: Can small helping exercises demonstrate trait change?

not_for: Do not use this page for clinical diagnosis or as the sole basis for hiring or admission.
method_boundary.summary: Use this page to understand personality concepts and examine everyday behavior. Interpret actual scores using the instrument’s scoring method, reference sample, and intended use.

sections.body:
Altruism is an Agreeableness facet in the NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary used here. It concerns attention to other people's needs, willingness to help and everyday ways of offering assistance or support. The item content includes both concern and interpersonal actions, such as welcoming others or making time for them. It is broader than a donation total, a completed-favor count or private goodwill alone.

A stronger tendency may appear in readily considering a concrete offer of help. A weaker tendency may involve less spontaneous interest in assisting, or a need for an explicit request before considering involvement. An intermediate position can include substantial variation between situations. These are continuous differences, not good, selfish and average personality types.

Helping can have several motives at once: concern, responsibility, habit, reciprocity or a wish for approval. You do not need to establish a perfectly selfless motive to recognize help, and an observed action does not reveal a person's entire motivation.
sections.heading: What readiness to help looks like

sections.body:
Willingness asks whether you want to respond. Capability asks whether you have the relevant skill or knowledge. Capacity asks whether time, energy and other resources are available now. Usefulness asks whether the assistance fits the recipient's needs and produces an appropriate result.

A willing helper can give unsuitable advice. A capable person may lack time. Declining a request does not independently establish indifference, and completing it successfully does not establish a generally strong helping tendency.

Sympathetic concern and readiness to help are related but distinct questions. Feeling moved does not guarantee action; acting does not require an intense emotional reaction. Trust concerns assumptions about another person's intentions, while Compliance concerns responses to conflict. You can verify a request or disagree with someone and still offer suitable assistance.

Boundaries are not a skill automatically supplied by lower Altruism, or automatically absent at the higher end. They depend on what you communicate and follow through on.
sections.heading: Willing, able and useful are different

sections.body:
At a community garden, Mina notices that donated seed packets need sorting. The coordinator confirms that help is welcome. Mina offers twenty minutes to sort labels, while explaining that she cannot store the remaining supplies or take on weekly coordination. The situation gives separate information about willingness, consent and available capacity.

It does not yet establish expertise or impact. Mina may enjoy sorting, feel responsible as a member, or want to welcome a newcomer. The labels may still need checking. Whether the help was useful depends on what actually happened and what the coordinator needed.

If Mina wanted to help but had to leave for another commitment, desire and action would diverge. If she reorganized the supplies without asking, substantial effort might still be unwanted. Amount of effort alone does not answer the question.
sections.heading: A concrete offer at a community garden

sections.body:
A specific working hypothesis could be: 'When someone welcomes a small contribution that I can manage, I usually offer concrete help.' The target behavior is making the offer, not having it accepted or producing a successful outcome.

On another occasion, a comparable sorting task is available, help is welcome and Mina has sufficient time and ability. She nevertheless chooses to read and makes no offer. That is an opportunity where the target behavior did not occur, and a natural exception to the same hypothesis.

One exception does not refute 'usually.' If such occasions repeatedly involve unfamiliar groups, the description may need narrowing. If the coordinator already has enough help, or Mina has no available capacity, the conditions of the hypothesis are absent; those are not equivalent counterexamples.

A person who initially expects little spontaneous helping should also include naturally occurring offers that surprise them. Neither a single offer nor a single refusal requires switching to a different personality type.
sections.heading: Keep natural exceptions inside the same question

sections.body:
Choose a recurring category of small requests in your own life. Record the need, whether help is welcome, your capability and spare capacity, your first reaction and whether you made a concrete offer. Keep wanting to help but being unable, having an opportunity but not offering, and having no suitable opportunity distinct. If you did not notice or cannot recall your wish to help, mark it as unknown rather than inferring it from the offer.

When an offer is made, separately record acceptance, what was actually done, its cost and whether it addressed the original need. Do not infer willingness backward from success or erase it because one attempt was ineffective. Ask whether the help was useful rather than inventing the recipient's feelings from a polite response.

After observing natural occasions, you might deliberately try asking what is wanted before offering a limited contribution. Keep arrangements that are working. If a commitment is too large or the assistance does not meet the need, discuss changing its scope, another form of help or ending it. You can decline a new attempt. Label these changes as intentional attempts. It tests clarity and feasibility in that situation; it does not establish a change in Altruism.

Comparable natural offers can support retaining the narrow hypothesis. A pattern restricted to familiar people or particular tasks calls for narrowing it. Missing opportunities, ambiguous requests or uncertain capability call for leaving it undecided. A short record is not a validation of a personality score.
sections.heading: Observe the offer, then assess the assistance

sections.body:
An offer can be specific: 'I can sort these packets for twenty minutes, but I cannot take the remaining supplies home.' A refusal can also be specific about what you cannot undertake. If you know a suitable source of help, ask whether the person wants that information. Referring someone elsewhere is an observable contribution, not automatically inferior to taking over.

Agreeing is not required to prove that you care. Consider your existing commitments, the recipient's autonomy and the request itself. Safety, privacy and tasks beyond your competence require direct judgment; a helping identity cannot override them.

If you rarely offer help spontaneously, an explicit small request can help you understand your willingness without accepting everything. If you often offer, look for continuing obligations that neither party has clearly discussed. Both positions benefit from actual communication, and neither establishes skill.
sections.heading: Make limits understandable

sections.body:
The [official IPIP comparison](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEO_FacetsTable.htm) identifies A3 as Altruism. The [longer item set](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOFacetsKey.htm) and [four-item version](https://ipip.ori.org/30FacetNEO-PI-RItems_Maples_etal.htm) include helping, concern and welcoming content. These support the construct vocabulary, not a judgment of your morality or effectiveness. Different Big Five inventories need not report the same standalone facets. This concept page does not establish that your selected test version measures or reports Altruism separately. Check the actual report and its scoring explanation; a domain score cannot supply an unreported facet score.

Read [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness) for the broader interpersonal context. [Tender-Mindedness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/tender-mindedness) addresses sympathetic concern, [Trust](/en/personality/big-five/facets/trust) addresses expectations about others, and [Compliance](/en/personality/big-five/facets/compliance) addresses conflict. The [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets) helps keep those questions distinct.
